name: Equal Chords and Angles at the Centre

scenes.animation: A round pizza with centre O. Zippy cuts two straight chords of the same length at different places; two 'slice angles' at the centre glow and a protractor pops up showing both are equal.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: I cut two equal chords in different places, and the angles at the centre came out the same. Magic?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Geometry. Equal chords always subtend equal angles at the centre.

scenes.animation: Circle with centre O and chord PQ. Radii OP and OQ are drawn, forming ∠POQ, labelled 'angle subtended by chord PQ at the centre'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: A chord is a line segment joining two points on a circle.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Join its ends to the centre O. The angle POQ is the angle subtended by the chord at the centre.

scenes.animation: Circle with centre O and equal chords AB and CD, ticked. Radii drawn to all four ends. Proof lines appear one by one: 'OA = OC (radii)', 'OB = OD (radii)', 'AB = CD (given)', '∴ △AOB ≅ △COD (SSS)', '∴ ∠AOB = ∠COD (CPCT)'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Theorem: equal chords of a circle subtend equal angles at the centre.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Let AB and CD be equal chords. In triangles AOB and COD, OA equals OC and OB equals OD, because all radii are equal. And AB equals CD, given.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: So the triangles are congruent by SSS, and angle AOB equals angle COD by CPCT.

scenes.animation: The theorem card flips to its converse: 'If the angles subtended by two chords at the centre are equal, the chords are equal'. Two equal angles at O glow and their chords stretch to identical lengths.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The converse is also true. If the angles subtended by two chords at the centre are equal, then the chords are equal.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: So equal chords give equal angles, and equal angles give equal chords. A two-way street!

scenes.animation: Worked example on a chalkboard: circle radius 5 cm, chord AB subtends ∠AOB = 60°. Lines build: 'OA = OB = 5 cm (radii)', '∠OAB = ∠OBA (angles opposite equal sides)', '∠OAB + ∠OBA = 180° − 60° = 120°', 'each = 60°', '△AOB is equilateral ⇒ AB = 5 cm'. An 'EXAM TIP' card slides in.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Example: in a circle of radius 5 centimetres, chord AB subtends 60 degrees at the centre. Find AB.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: OA and OB are radii, so both are 5 centimetres. The base angles of triangle AOB are equal.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Together they make 180 minus 60, which is 120 degrees. So each is 60 degrees.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: All angles are 60 degrees, so the triangle is equilateral and AB is 5 centimetres.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exam tip: in circle proofs, always look for radii first. They give you free equal sides.

scenes.animation: Recap board with the pizza icon: '1. Angle subtended at centre: join chord ends to O', '2. Equal chords ⇒ equal angles at centre (SSS)', '3. Equal angles at centre ⇒ equal chords'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: join the ends of a chord to the centre to get the angle it subtends.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: equal chords subtend equal angles at the centre, proved by SSS.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: chords that subtend equal angles at the centre are equal.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Equal slices for everyone. Geometry is fair!

name: Perpendicular from the Centre to a Chord

scenes.animation: A round well in a village. A bucket rope hangs from the centre of a wooden beam laid across the well like a chord; Zippy notices the rope hits the beam exactly at its middle.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: The rope from the centre drops straight down and lands exactly at the middle of the beam. Always?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Always, if the line from the centre is perpendicular to the chord. Let's prove it.

scenes.animation: Circle with centre O and chord AB. OM is drawn perpendicular to AB with a right-angle box at M. Proof lines: '∠OMA = ∠OMB = 90°', 'OA = OB (radii)', 'OM = OM (common)', '∴ △OMA ≅ △OMB (RHS)', '∴ AM = BM (CPCT)'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Theorem: the perpendicular from the centre of a circle to a chord bisects the chord.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Draw OM perpendicular to chord AB, and join OA and OB.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: In triangles OMA and OMB, both angles at M are 90 degrees. OA equals OB, as radii. OM is common.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: So the triangles are congruent by RHS, and AM equals BM by CPCT.

scenes.animation: The theorem card flips to the converse: 'The line drawn through the centre to bisect a chord is perpendicular to the chord'. A line from O hits the midpoint M and a right-angle box snaps into place.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The converse: the line drawn through the centre of a circle to bisect a chord is perpendicular to the chord.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: So centre plus midpoint means right angle, and centre plus right angle means midpoint.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exactly right.

scenes.animation: Worked example: circle radius 5 cm, chord AB = 8 cm. Lines build: 'AM = 8 ÷ 2 = 4 cm (perpendicular bisects chord)', 'OM² = OA² − AM²', 'OM² = 5² − 4² = 25 − 16 = 9', 'OM = 3 cm'. The right triangle OMA glows.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Example: a chord of length 8 centimetres is drawn in a circle of radius 5 centimetres. How far is it from the centre?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The perpendicular OM bisects the chord, so AM is 4 centimetres.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: In right triangle OMA, OM squared is 5 squared minus 4 squared, which is 25 minus 16, or 9. So OM is 3 centimetres.

scenes.animation: A second quick example flashes: 'r = 13 cm, distance = 5 cm', 'half-chord² = 169 − 25 = 144', 'half-chord = 12 cm', 'chord = 24 cm'. An 'EXAM TIP' card reads 'Don't forget to double the half-chord'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Reverse it. Radius 13 centimetres, chord 5 centimetres from the centre.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Half the chord squared is 169 minus 25, which is 144. So half the chord is 12, and the chord is 24 centimetres.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exam tip: Pythagoras gives you half the chord. Students often forget to double it.

scenes.animation: Recap board with the well icon: '1. Perpendicular from centre bisects the chord (RHS)', '2. Line from centre to mid-point of chord is perpendicular to it', '3. radius² = (half-chord)² + distance²'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: the perpendicular from the centre to a chord bisects it.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: the line from the centre that bisects a chord is perpendicular to it.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: radius squared equals half-chord squared plus distance squared.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: The well rope knew this all along.

name: Equal Chords and Their Distances from the Centre

scenes.animation: A round chapati on a tawa. Zippy places two equal-length breadsticks across it at different spots; tiny measuring tapes shoot from the centre to each breadstick and show the same reading.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Two equal breadsticks, placed anywhere, and both are the same distance from the centre. Suspicious!

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Not suspicious. It's a theorem. First, let's define distance properly.

scenes.animation: From a point P, several slanted segments reach a line; the perpendicular one glows green and is labelled 'shortest = distance'. Then in a circle, OM ⊥ chord AB is labelled 'distance of chord from centre'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The distance of a point from a line is the length of the perpendicular from the point to the line. It is the shortest of all segments.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: So the distance of a chord from the centre is the length of the perpendicular from the centre to the chord.

scenes.animation: Circle with equal chords AB and CD, perpendiculars OM and ON drawn. Proof builds line by line: 'AM = ½ AB, CN = ½ CD (perpendicular bisects chord)', 'AB = CD ⇒ AM = CN', 'OA = OC (radii)', '∠OMA = ∠ONC = 90°', '∴ △OMA ≅ △ONC (RHS)', '∴ OM = ON (CPCT)'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Theorem: equal chords of a circle are equidistant from the centre.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Draw OM perpendicular to AB and ON perpendicular to CD. These perpendiculars bisect the chords, so AM equals CN.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: OA equals OC, as radii, and both angles at M and N are 90 degrees.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: So triangles OMA and ONC are congruent by RHS, and OM equals ON by CPCT.

scenes.animation: The card flips to the converse: 'Chords equidistant from the centre are equal in length'. Then a longer chord slides closer to the centre while a shorter chord drifts outward, as a fun visual.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The converse is also true: chords equidistant from the centre of a circle are equal in length.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: And I notice longer chords sit closer to the centre.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Good observation. The longest chord, the diameter, passes through the centre itself.

scenes.animation: Worked example: circle radius 10 cm with two chords of 16 cm each. Lines build: 'half-chord = 16 ÷ 2 = 8 cm', 'distance² = 10² − 8² = 100 − 64 = 36', 'distance = 6 cm', 'Both chords are 6 cm from O ✓'. An 'EXAM TIP' card appears.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Example: a circle has radius 10 centimetres. Two chords are each 16 centimetres long. How far is each from the centre?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Half of each chord is 8 centimetres. Distance squared is 10 squared minus 8 squared, which is 100 minus 64, or 36.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: So the distance is 6 centimetres, the same for both chords, just as the theorem says.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exam tip: always draw the perpendicular from the centre before you calculate. It earns the figure mark.

scenes.animation: Recap board with the chapati icon: '1. Distance of chord = perpendicular from centre', '2. Equal chords are equidistant from the centre', '3. Equidistant chords are equal'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: the distance of a chord from the centre is measured along the perpendicular.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: equal chords are equidistant from the centre.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: chords equidistant from the centre are equal.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Breadsticks: equal, equidistant, and delicious.

scenes.animation: A circular cricket ground. The two stumps at one end are points B and C on the boundary. Neo stands at the centre O, Zippy stands on the boundary at A; each holds a protractor aimed at the stumps. Neo's reads 80°, Zippy's reads 40°.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: We are looking at the same two stumps, but your angle is double mine!

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Because I'm at the centre. The angle at the centre is always double.

scenes.animation: Circle with arc BC highlighted in orange, ∠BOC at the centre and ∠BAC at point A on the remaining part of the circle. Theorem box: '∠BOC = 2 ∠BAC'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Theorem: the angle subtended by an arc at the centre is double the angle subtended by it at any point on the remaining part of the circle.

scenes.animation: Proof builds step by step: AO is joined and extended to D. Lines: 'OA = OB (radii) ⇒ ∠OAB = ∠OBA', '∠BOD = ∠OAB + ∠OBA = 2∠OAB (exterior angle)', 'Similarly ∠DOC = 2∠OAC', 'Adding: ∠BOC = 2(∠OAB + ∠OAC) = 2∠BAC'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Join AO and extend it to a point D.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: In triangle OAB, OA equals OB, so angle OAB equals angle OBA. The exterior angle BOD equals their sum, which is twice angle OAB.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: In the same way, angle DOC is twice angle OAC.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Adding, angle BOC is twice angle BAC. Proved.

scenes.animation: Several points A, D, E on the same arc all look at chord BC; their angles glow the same colour. Card: 'Angles in the same segment are equal'. Then BC becomes a diameter and every angle turns into a right-angle box: 'Angle in a semicircle = 90°'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Every point on the remaining arc gets half of the same central angle. So angles in the same segment of a circle are equal.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: What if the chord is a diameter?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Then the central angle is 180 degrees, so the angle in a semicircle is 90 degrees.

scenes.animation: Worked example: circle with points A, B, C, D; ∠ABC = 69°, ∠ACB = 31°, find ∠BDC. Lines build: '∠BAC = 180° − 69° − 31° = 80°', '∠BDC = ∠BAC (same segment)', '∠BDC = 80°'. An 'EXAM TIP' card appears.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Example: A, B, C and D lie on a circle. Angle ABC is 69 degrees and angle ACB is 31 degrees. Find angle BDC.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: In triangle ABC, angle BAC is 180 minus 69 minus 31, which is 80 degrees.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Angles BAC and BDC are in the same segment, so angle BDC is also 80 degrees.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exam tip: check that both angles stand on the same chord and lie on the same side of it before calling them equal.

scenes.animation: Recap board with the cricket ground: '1. Angle at centre = 2 × angle at remaining circle', '2. Angles in the same segment are equal', '3. Angle in a semicircle = 90°'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: the angle at the centre is double the angle at any point on the remaining part of the circle.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: angles in the same segment are equal.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: the angle in a semicircle is a right angle.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Next match, I'm fielding at the centre.

scenes.animation: Four children stand on a circular rangoli border holding a rope stretched into a quadrilateral. Zippy measures two opposite corners: 70° and 110°, then two others: 95° and 85°. A '180!' sparkles each time.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Opposite corners of our rope keep adding up to 180. Every single time!

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Because all four corners are on a circle. That makes it a cyclic quadrilateral.

scenes.animation: Circle with quadrilateral ABCD, all four vertices glowing on the circle. Label 'Cyclic quadrilateral: all four vertices lie on a circle'. Theorem box: '∠A + ∠C = 180°, ∠B + ∠D = 180°'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: A quadrilateral is cyclic if all four of its vertices lie on a circle.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Theorem: the sum of either pair of opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral is 180 degrees.

scenes.animation: Proof builds step by step: centre O is joined to B and D. The minor angle BOD and the reflex angle BOD glow in two colours. Lines: '∠BOD = 2∠A (arc BCD)', 'reflex ∠BOD = 2∠C (arc BAD)', '2∠A + 2∠C = 360°', '∠A + ∠C = 180°'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Join the centre O to B and D.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Arc BCD subtends angle BOD at the centre and angle A on the circle. So angle BOD is twice angle A.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Arc BAD subtends the reflex angle BOD at the centre and angle C on the circle. So the reflex angle is twice angle C.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The two angles at O make 360 degrees. So twice A plus twice C is 360, and A plus C is 180.

scenes.animation: The theorem card flips to the converse: 'If a pair of opposite angles of a quadrilateral sums to 180°, it is cyclic'. A wobbly quadrilateral with opposite angles 100° and 80° snaps onto a circle.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The converse is also true. If the sum of a pair of opposite angles of a quadrilateral is 180 degrees, the quadrilateral is cyclic.

scenes.animation: Worked example: cyclic ABCD with diagonals; ∠DBC = 55°, ∠BAC = 45°. Lines build: '∠CAD = ∠DBC = 55° (same segment)', '∠BAD = ∠BAC + ∠CAD = 45° + 55° = 100°', '∠BCD = 180° − 100° = 80° (opposite angles)'. An 'EXAM TIP' card appears.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Example: ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral. Angle DBC is 55 degrees and angle BAC is 45 degrees. Find angle BCD.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Angles CAD and DBC stand on chord CD in the same segment, so angle CAD is 55 degrees.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: So angle BAD is 45 plus 55, which is 100 degrees.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Angle BCD is opposite angle BAD, so it is 180 minus 100, which is 80 degrees.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Two theorems in one question. Sneaky!

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exam tip: exam questions often combine same-segment angles with the cyclic quadrilateral rule. Look for both.

scenes.animation: Recap board with the rangoli rope: '1. Cyclic quadrilateral: all vertices on a circle', '2. Opposite angles add to 180°', '3. Converse: opposite angles sum 180° ⇒ cyclic'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: a cyclic quadrilateral has all four vertices on a circle.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: each pair of its opposite angles adds up to 180 degrees.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: if a pair of opposite angles adds up to 180 degrees, the quadrilateral is cyclic.
